title: Miss Cole's place and jobs her husband avoided
summary: Miss Cole's big place where bands played, her husband's dislike of rough jobs, and a nephew's newspaper story.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: She had all those long parties.
Yeah, she was a spiritual, too, you know. What was it, Third and Willow?

And she was the woman that they say used to insure so many people, and then they caught on to her, and they would die right now. She had that lawn place up there. It was on Willow, wasn't it? Yeah, I think it was somewhere back there. How do you call them? Miss Cole, her name was Miss Cole, and she had that big place on the corner of Willow and some of them street back Magnolia or something. I don't know the streets much, you know. I know how to get to them, but I hardly ever keep them in mind, too.
Kid Bunch tells me about that.

Yeah, they had a lot of the bands used to, you know, all the bands used to go in there and play. Of course, she made plenty of money, that woman, but there was different kind of people from the people down here. They always select, you know, the Creole people. And of course, I was a different set. We'd more like go to espionage, you know, just to see, to find out something. We wouldn't go into maybe a dance. My brother used to take me anywhere, and I'd take a good look, sis, and we'd look around and see. We'd just walk in there like overseas and walk out. We'd just like to go and see, you know. I'd like my children to do that right now, go see some things just to know. It's always good to know, you know. And she raised plenty of money on that place, you know. Yes, indeed. Well, you see them kind of jobs where your daddy didn't go for that too much. Them kind would pull them tanky people. He was one man, he liked a different one. I said, who was that? He ain't no fighter. Well, he sure wasn't a fighter, you know. Like they told Uncle Chum that time, he said, go stop that fight. Chum, one of my nephews, you know, been in a place for years, a bartender, and he called him Chum, you know. And he said, go stop that fight. And they just put that on the paper because they figured his wife was jealous, you know. And he said he wasn't a fighting man, he was a lover man. But he said, no, no. He didn't say that. And I know my nephew didn't say that because he's very timid and very, you know, refined. He wouldn't want us to maybe, and I read it. And they said, and I know he didn't say that, but his wife is jealous, you see. And they said it done that to make her jealous, you know. They put it in the paper? Yeah. They said they told him to go stop the fight and say he wasn't no fighting man, he was a lover man. Big headline on the Louisiana week that they had that on the paper. And that was his, so anyhow, their daddy was, I don't guess he ever had any fights when he was a little child or something. He said Uncle Rudolph is like that, Uncle Todd used to like to fight Nick, and Uncle Dave wouldn't date nothing. But Uncle Rudolph and your dad, it was, they all, everybody, the family always put them select, you know. They was different.
